Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Shear stress calculator work?
sections.html:
The Shear stress calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports moment of inertia (I) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of load, the beam cross-section and the shaft cross-section); then you type in the shear force magnitude (V), the width (t), the first moment of area (Q = ȳ'A') and the square height (d).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Shear stress calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Moment of inertia (I)=shear force magnitude (V) × first moment of area (Q = ȳ'A') ÷ (shear stress magnitude (𝜏) × width (t))
Area (A)=(3 ÷ 2) × shear force magnitude (V) ÷ maximum shear stress magnitude (𝜏ₘₐₓ)
Shear stress magnitude at distance y (𝜏)=(3 ÷ 2) × shear force magnitude (V) × ((square height (d) ^ 2) − 4 × (distance to the neutral axis (y) ^ 2)) ÷ (area (A) × (square height (d) ^ 2))
Area (A)=base width (b) × square height (d)
Maximum shear stress magnitude (𝜏ₘₐₓ)=((4 ÷ 3) × shear force magnitude (V) × ((outer radius (R) ^ 2) + outer radius (R) × inner radius (Rᵢ) + (inner radius (Rᵢ) ^ 2)) ÷ (a hollow circle × ((outer radius (R) ^ 2) + (inner radius (Rᵢ) ^ 2))))
A hollow circle=PI × ((outer radius (R) ^ 2) − (inner radius (Rᵢ) ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Second moment of area, opening in quartic meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Torque, opening in newton meters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Shear stress calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the shear force magnitude, the width and the first moment of area — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Shear stress calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns moment of inertia (I), derived from the shear force magnitude, the width and the first moment of area. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Shear stress calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the shear force magnitude, the width, the first moment of area and the square height, which is 15 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter shear force magnitude (V) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Shear force magnitude (V) opens in newtons and the chip beside it offers 16 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Shear stress calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
